hook: Read this one on a full screen and take your time, because the formatting is part of the experience. It presents itself as a classified file that has to check whether you are fit to read it, and that framing becomes the story. It is about corpses floating in a lake, but its power is psychological rather than graphic.
whyItMatters: It is a strong example of the meta-styled cognitohazard article, where the document behaves as though it is reacting to the person reading it. The interactive format and the quiet grief underneath it work together, which is a big part of why it stays with readers.
thingsToNotice:
The repeated phrase works like a mantra the file needs you to accept, and each repetition sounds less like a fact and more like an order. Watch the intrusions: footnotes that argue with the main text and start listing names, automated edits that lock them out, and an interviewee whose speaker label slowly turns into the mantra and then into "Me".

The reveal is that the bodies are a high school class who visited that lake on a school outing in autumn 1975, and the interrupting voice insists that you, the reader, were one of them and one of only two who got away. In the interview, the agent who walked into the lake starts naming the school, and Dr. Harrison has them dragged off for amnestics and the recorder shut off; the footnotes claim the Foundation saw what was happening to the kids and let it happen, and that the cognitohazard is really the dead calling for help. Once your verification fails, the file stops being a report and becomes a plea to go back into the water, so the final question is whether that voice is a witness telling the truth or the lake reaching for one more person.
